chunks: Common IC packages and trade-offs. The question: What are some common IC packages? What are their tradeoffs?
An IC (integrated circuit, or chip) package is the case around the chip. It protects the chip, connects its tiny contacts to pads on the board, and carries heat away.
Packages come in a few families (legs, flat pads, a grid of solder balls), and each trades off pin count, size, heat, and ease of soldering and inspection.
Think of parking cars. A package with legs around its edge is like parking along the curb: you can see every car, but only so many fit.
A ball grid is like a full parking lot: many more cars fit in the same area.
The catch is that cars in the middle are hidden from view and hard to get out, just as ball connections under a package are hard to inspect and repair.
A package decision usually starts with pin count and power, then asks about assembly capability.
Notice that prototype-friendliness can override density; many chips are offered in several packages for exactly that reason.
Package: the case around the chip, with the connections to the board. Pitch: the center-to-center spacing between neighboring pins or balls. Through-hole vs.
surface-mount: legs pushed through holes in the board, or contacts soldered flat onto pads on the surface.
QFN: a flat package with contacts on its underside edges and no legs sticking out. BGA: a package with a grid of solder balls underneath.
Exposed pad: a metal plate on the underside, soldered to the board to carry heat away.
Take a square body 10 mm on a side. Put pins around the edge at 0. 5 mm pitch. You get about 4 times 10 ÷ 0. 5 = 80 pins. Now fill the underside with balls at the same 0.
5 mm pitch. You get (10 ÷ 0. 5)² = 20 times 20 = 400 balls. The grid wins because its count grows with the area, while edge pins grow only with the perimeter.
Real parts have fewer. That is the whole idea.

"Packages fall into families: through-hole like DIP and TO-220, leaded SMD like SOIC and QFP, leadless like QFN with an exposed pad, area-array BGAs with balls under the package, and wafer-level or stacked packages for phones.
Moving along that list gives more pins per area, lower inductance and better thermals, but harder inspection, rework and PCB routing.
I choose by pin count, heat, speed and what my assembly process can handle, and use the hand-friendly option for prototypes."
